title: Node.js, npm, Vite, and Project Tooling
description: Understand where Node.js fits in frontend work, how package.json and lockfiles describe dependencies, how npm scripts and Vite support the development loop, and how linting and formatting improve consistency.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish the browser JavaScript runtime from the Node.js runtime.
Explain the purpose of package.json, dependency categories, package versions, and a lockfile.
Choose npm install or npm ci for the appropriate workflow.
Use npm scripts to start, test, lint, typecheck, and build a project.
Explain the roles of Vite, ESLint, and Prettier without treating them as interchangeable.
Create a reproducible project setup and verify it using package scripts.
Distinguish installing a dependency, running a package CLI with npx/npm exec, and scaffolding with npm create.

blocks.text: A frontend project is more than source files

A React or TypeScript project depends on a development environment as well as application code. The runtime executes JavaScript, the package manager obtains dependencies, the build tool serves files and produces output, and quality tools detect common problems or normalize formatting. These tools solve different problems and are usually coordinated through project scripts so that team members and CI can repeat the same workflow.
Node.js: JavaScript outside the browser

Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on the V8 engine and a set of runtime APIs. It allows JavaScript programs to run outside the browser, which is why frontend development tools such as Vite, ESLint, and many package scripts run through Node. The browser and Node do not expose the same APIs: document and window belong to browser contexts, while Node exposes APIs for processes, files, modules, and other server-side or tooling tasks.

blocks.caption: Check the installed runtime and package manager
blocks.code:
node --version
npm --version
node -e "console.log('Node is running JavaScript')"

blocks.text: package.json describes the project contract

package.json contains project metadata and configuration such as scripts, dependencies, development dependencies, and package constraints. A dependency is code the project needs. The distinction between dependencies and devDependencies is a practical classification for installation and packaging—not an absolute security boundary. Frontend build/test/lint tooling is commonly placed under devDependencies, while packages imported by the application at runtime are commonly dependencies.

steps.title: Describe the package
steps.explanation: name identifies the package, and private:true prevents accidental publication to the public npm registry. These fields describe the project rather than its application UI.

steps.title: Expose repeatable commands
steps.explanation: Scripts give meaningful names to tool commands. Team members and CI can call npm run build instead of remembering the exact command and flags.

steps.title: Separate runtime and development packages
steps.explanation: React is shown as an application dependency, while Vite and TypeScript are shown as development tools. Real projects choose the category based on how the package is used and deployed.

blocks.text: The lockfile makes installs more reproducible

A package manifest often contains version ranges, such as ^18.3.1. A lockfile records the resolved dependency tree and integrity information so a team or CI can recreate the same dependency graph. Commit the lockfile for an application. Do not hand-edit it to force a version: change the package through the package manager, inspect the resulting diff, and test it.
npm install versus npm ci

items: npm install installs dependencies and can update the lockfile when the manifest and lockfile need to be reconciled.
npm ci is intended for clean, repeatable automated installs. It requires a lockfile that matches package.json and removes the existing node_modules before installing.
node_modules is generated output and normally belongs in .gitignore, not in the repository.
The lockfile should normally be committed; local caches and installed package files should not.

blocks.text: Version ranges and package-manager choices

Exact versions, caret ranges such as ^1.2.3, and tilde ranges such as ~1.2.3 communicate different update policies. For normal stable semantic versions, caret generally permits compatible minor and patch updates within the same major, while tilde generally stays within the same minor. Prereleases and zero-major packages have important edge cases, so verify the actual range rather than relying on shorthand memory. npm, Yarn, and pnpm are package managers; a project should document and standardize one package manager and its lockfile rather than casually mixing them.
Use scripts as the project workflow

npm run invokes a script defined by the project. Typical scripts start the development server, build production assets, run tests, lint files, check types, and format source. The exact scripts are project-specific. A README should document the main commands and their expected use so a new developer can reproduce the workflow.
npm install, npx/npm exec, and npm create do different jobs

In normal project use, `npm install <package>` adds a dependency to the project manifest and updates the lockfile; use `-D` for a development dependency. `npx <command>` is implemented by modern npm through `npm exec`: it runs a package CLI, using a locally installed executable when available. If the package is missing locally, npm may fetch it into its cache and ask for permission; invoking it does not automatically add it as a lasting project dependency. `npm create` / `npm init` runs a package initializer to scaffold a project. For repeatable team scripts and CI, declare the required tool and run it through `package.json` scripts rather than depending on an unpinned, on-demand CLI. Treat an unfamiliar CLI package as code you are about to execute.

blocks.code:
# Inspect scripts configured for this repository
npm run

# Run a project CLI when Vite is declared as a dependency
npm exec -- vite --version

# Scaffold a new project in a new directory
npm create vite@latest my-app

steps.title: Inspect the project scripts
steps.explanation: Running `npm run` without a script name lists the scripts declared in package.json. Read that contract and the chosen lockfile before copying commands from a tutorial.

steps.title: Run a CLI through npm exec
steps.explanation: When Vite is installed in the current project, npm exec can invoke its local binary. The `--` separates npm's own options from the command's arguments. If a package is not installed locally, npm may fetch it into its cache and prompt; verify the package and version before approving execution.

steps.title: Scaffold with npm create
steps.explanation: The create alias runs a package initializer that can generate project files and may ask interactive questions. Review the requested package/version and target directory first; do not run a scaffolder blindly over an existing project.

blocks.prompt: Which statement accurately describes `npx` / `npm exec` in modern npm?

options.text: It runs a package's CLI; a missing package may be fetched into npm's cache, but invoking it does not automatically add a permanent dependency entry.
options.feedback: Correct. npm exec uses a suitable local executable when available and can fetch a missing CLI for execution. That does not mean the package is now declared in package.json.

options.text: It always adds the package to dependencies and updates package-lock.json like npm install.
options.feedback: Running a CLI through npm exec does not by itself declare a lasting project dependency; use npm install when that is the intention.

options.text: It installs every CLI globally and keeps the executable available to all projects.
options.feedback: npx/npm exec is not a synonym for a global install. Global installation changes the machine environment and is not needed for every CLI invocation.

options.text: It is the same as npm create and always generates a new project directory.
options.feedback: npm create runs an initializer to scaffold a project; npm exec runs a selected package executable. They serve related but different tasks.

blocks.explanation: Use install to declare dependencies, exec/npx to run a CLI, and create/init to run a scaffolder. For reproducible team workflows, keep required tools and versions declared in the project.

blocks.text: What Vite does

Vite provides a development server with fast feedback and a production build pipeline. During development it serves source modules and uses browser-native ES module support with transformation where needed. For production it bundles and optimizes assets. Vite is not the JavaScript runtime itself and is not a package manager; it uses Node and installed dependencies to perform its work.
ESLint and Prettier solve different problems

ESLint analyzes source code for configurable correctness, maintainability, and risky-pattern rules. Prettier formats source into a consistent layout according to its formatting rules. They can be used together: use ESLint to identify code patterns worth fixing and Prettier to normalize formatting. Formatting cannot prove that code is correct, and linting is not a replacement for tests or type checking.

blocks.code:
npm ci
npm run dev
# implement a change
npm run lint
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run build

steps.title: Recreate the dependency tree
steps.explanation: npm ci uses the committed lockfile to perform a clean install. If manifest and lockfile disagree, fix that mismatch rather than bypassing the failure.

steps.title: Start the development environment
steps.explanation: npm run dev invokes the project's dev script, which usually starts Vite and reports a local URL.

steps.title: Run automated quality gates
steps.explanation: Lint, typecheck and tests answer different questions. Run the actual scripts configured by the repository; not every project uses the same script names or test framework.

steps.title: Verify the production build
steps.explanation: A successful development server does not guarantee the production build succeeds. The build validates another part of the delivery path.

blocks.title: Do not solve dependency problems by deleting the lockfile first
blocks.text: A lockfile captures the exact dependency graph. Deleting it can produce a large unrelated dependency update and make a failure difficult to reproduce. Inspect the error, package versions and lockfile diff before deciding whether regeneration is appropriate.

blocks.prompt: What is the main role of a package-lock.json file in a typical npm application?

options.text: Record resolved dependency versions and integrity information
options.feedback: The lockfile captures a resolved dependency graph to support repeatable installs.

options.text: Store the application's production user data
options.feedback: Application data belongs to an application storage system or database, not the dependency lockfile.

options.text: Define the HTML routes of a React application
options.feedback: Routes are defined in application code or routing configuration; the lockfile records package resolutions.
The manifest describes dependencies/scripts while the lockfile records their resolved installation graph; the two serve different roles.

blocks.explanation: package.json describes the project and intended dependency ranges; the lockfile records the resolved tree used for installations.

blocks.prompt: Vite is both the JavaScript runtime and the package manager in a typical React project.

options.feedback: Vite is a development server and build tool. Node.js runs the tooling, while npm/Yarn/pnpm manage installed packages.
The runtime, package manager, and build tool have distinct responsibilities even when scripts combine them into one workflow.

blocks.explanation: Node.js executes tooling, the package manager installs dependencies, and Vite serves and builds the application.

blocks.prompt: Which statements about project tooling are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: npm ci is useful for clean installs in CI
options.feedback: npm ci installs from the lockfile and fails when the manifest and lockfile are inconsistent.

options.text: ESLint and Prettier have identical purposes
options.feedback: ESLint analyzes code against rules; Prettier formats it consistently.

options.text: node_modules is normally generated and should usually be ignored by Git
options.feedback: Installed dependency files are recreated from the package manifest and lockfile rather than committed in a typical application.

options.text: A successful dev server guarantees that the production build will succeed
options.feedback: The production build has its own bundling and validation steps and can fail even when development mode works.

blocks.explanation: Reproducible installation, linting, formatting, and production builds are complementary rather than interchangeable.

blocks.title: Set up and document a reproducible frontend project
blocks.context: Use the repository or a small practice project. The editor saves your command notes but does not execute shell commands. Run the commands in your own terminal and record what you observe.
instructions: Create or inspect a small Vite project and identify Node/npm versions.
Inspect package.json and identify scripts, dependencies and devDependencies.
Confirm that the lockfile is committed and node_modules is ignored.
Run npm ci, then start the project using the documented development script.
Run the available lint, typecheck, test and production build scripts; note which scripts are missing rather than inventing their results.

The manifest and lockfile are both understood and used for installation.
Generated dependencies and secrets are not committed.

node --version
npm --version

# Inspect project configuration
cat package.json

# Install exactly from the lockfile

# Check which scripts are configured before running them

# Then run the available scripts, for example:
# npm run dev
# npm run lint
# npm run typecheck

Do not assume every project already has lint, typecheck, and test scripts; add them intentionally and document their purpose.
Review lockfile changes as dependency changes, not as meaningless generated noise.

Generated and secret files are excluded from Git.

items: Node.js runs JavaScript tooling outside the browser; npm installs packages and runs project scripts.
package.json declares the project and dependency ranges; the lockfile records the resolved tree.
Vite serves development modules and produces a production build, while ESLint and Prettier serve different code-quality roles.
Use status checks and documented npm scripts to make the workflow reproducible.
Inspect dependency and lockfile changes, and do not commit node_modules or secrets.

blocks.text: Deep dive: lockfiles, reproducible installs, and frontend environment variables

`package.json` describes the package and allowed dependency ranges; the lockfile records the concrete dependency tree resolved for an installation. `npm install` can reconcile and update that lockfile, while `npm ci` is intended for clean, reproducible automated installs and fails when the lockfile disagrees with package.json. Vite's development server and production build are different modes: do not assume code that works in dev has been emitted and configured correctly for production.

steps.title: Scripts make project tasks reproducible
steps.explanation: Team members and CI can run the same named tasks instead of remembering local commands. Check the actual repository scripts rather than assuming these example names exist unchanged.

steps.title: Separate app libraries from build-time tools
steps.explanation: React is used by the app; Vite and TypeScript are commonly build/development tools. Exact classification depends on what the deployed runtime actually executes.

steps.title: Let the lockfile record the resolution
steps.explanation: Version ranges in package.json are not a complete record of the full dependency graph. Commit the lockfile so local installs and CI resolve a consistent tree.

items: `npm install` is useful while changing dependencies and may update package-lock.json to match package.json and the current resolver.
`npm ci` removes an existing node_modules directory, installs from the lockfile, and fails if package metadata and lockfile are inconsistent; it is useful in CI.
Commit package-lock.json for an application using npm. Do not edit lockfile internals by hand; change package metadata with npm and review the diff.
SemVer ranges express acceptable updates, not the exact full tree. A lockfile improves reproducibility but does not replace dependency review or vulnerability checks.
Vite variables prefixed with `VITE_` are exposed to client-side code and can be included in the built bundle. Never use that prefix for passwords, private API keys, or other secrets.

blocks.title: A frontend environment variable is not secret storage
blocks.text: The browser must receive client-side values to use them, so `VITE_*` variables should be treated as public. Sensitive server credentials belong in a trusted server or deployment secret store, never in the code sent to users.

blocks.prompt: A CI job needs a clean install that follows the committed npm lockfile and fails if the lockfile is out of sync. Which command is designed for this?

options.feedback: npm ci performs a clean install from the lockfile and rejects a mismatch with package metadata.
Update intentionally moves dependency versions within allowed ranges and is not the reproducible-install command.
This can change dependency versions to address audit findings and is not a deterministic lockfile install.
Removing the lockfile loses the committed resolution and allows dependency versions to be resolved anew.

blocks.explanation: Use the correct install command for the purpose: dependency changes locally versus reproducible installation in CI.

blocks.title: Make a project install reproducibly and audit public configuration
blocks.context: Prepare a Vite/TypeScript project for team work and CI; do not put credentials into client-side configuration.
instructions: Inspect package.json and package-lock.json and explain their different roles.
Run npm ci from a clean checkout and identify what a lockfile mismatch means.
Review scripts and ensure the documented build, test and lint commands match the project.
Inspect Vite environment variable usage and classify which values are public versus secret.
Review a dependency update diff before committing the package metadata and lockfile together.
requirements: Lockfile is versioned and treated as generated dependency resolution metadata.
Install command matches the CI reproducibility goal.
Scripts are verified against actual project configuration.
No secret is exposed through a VITE_ variable or committed frontend file.
Dependency changes are reviewed for scope and compatibility.

# Inspect the project first
cat package.json
git status --short
npm ci

# Then inspect the documented scripts and Vite env usage.
# Do not print or share actual secret values.
hints: package.json defines acceptable package ranges and project scripts; package-lock.json records the resolved tree.
npm ci expects lockfile consistency and is intended for automated clean installation.
Any value bundled into browser JavaScript should be considered public.
successCriteria: Uses npm ci for a clean reproducible install.
Identifies out-of-sync lockfile as a dependency metadata problem.
Separates public build configuration from server-side secrets.
Documents reviewed script and dependency changes.

items: Version ranges and lockfiles have related but different roles: acceptable versions versus a concrete resolved dependency tree.
Use npm ci for clean CI installs and npm install when deliberately changing dependency metadata.
Vite-prefixed client variables are public; build success and correct production configuration both need verification.
